dx: Folate deficiency megaloblastic anemia in a woman with alcohol use disorder
case: A 46-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder comes to the physician because of fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion for 3 months. She drinks about a pint of vodka daily and eats little besides crackers and coffee. She has glossitis and pale conjunctivae. Vibration sense, position sense, and gait are normal. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 8.9 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), MCV of 112 fL (80 to 100), reticulocyte count of 0.8% (0.5 to 2.5), leukocyte count of 3,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), and platelet count of 128,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). Serum folate is 1.8 ng/mL (above 4.0), and serum vitamin B12 is 520 pg/mL (200 to 900). The diagnosis is megaloblastic anemia from folate deficiency.

questions.stem: Macrocytosis in people who drink heavily can also occur without megaloblastic change. Which of the following findings on her peripheral blood smear would best indicate that her macrocytosis is megaloblastic?
options: Round macrocytes with target cells
Polychromatophilic macrocytes after bleeding
Neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes
Stomatocytes with slit-like central pallor
approach: Separate megaloblastic macrocytosis (impaired DNA synthesis) from nonmegaloblastic macrocytosis (membrane lipid change or young cells).
Ask which finding reflects slowed DNA synthesis in every dividing marrow line.
Hypersegmented neutrophils point to a megaloblastic process.
questions.why: Folate deficiency slows DNA synthesis in all rapidly dividing marrow cells, so nuclear maturation lags behind the cytoplasm. In the granulocyte line this produces neutrophils with six or more lobes, or more than 5% with five lobes. Oval macrocytes plus hypersegmented neutrophils mark megaloblastic anemia. Alcohol and liver disease enlarge red cells by changing membrane lipids, without nuclear changes in neutrophils.
whyNot: Round macrocytes and target cells come from extra membrane cholesterol and phospholipid in liver disease, a nonmegaloblastic cause.
Polychromatophilic cells are large reticulocytes. They raise the MCV after bleeding or hemolysis, without megaloblastic change.
Correct.
Stomatocytes are seen with heavy alcohol use and liver disease. They reflect membrane change, not impaired DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: Her serum methylmalonic acid concentration is normal, and her serum homocysteine concentration is increased. Which of the following reactions is most directly impaired, causing the megaloblastic changes in her erythroid precursors?
options: dUMP to dTMP by thymidylate synthase
Methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
Ribonucleotide reduction to deoxyribonucleotides
Orotic acid to UMP by UMP synthase
approach: Normal methylmalonic acid with high homocysteine points to folate deficiency, not B12 deficiency.
Folate, as N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate, donates the methyl group that turns dUMP into dTMP.
Without enough thymidine, DNA synthesis slows and cells become megaloblastic.
questions.why: Thymidylate synthase uses N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate to methylate dUMP to dTMP, the thymidine nucleotide needed for DNA. Folate deficiency limits this step, so DNA synthesis slows while RNA and hemoglobin synthesis continue, producing large cells with immature nuclei. Homocysteine rises because methionine synthase also needs a folate (N5-methyl tetrahydrofolate) donor. Methylmalonic acid stays normal because methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs B12, not folate.
whyNot: Correct.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs vitamin B12 only. Its failure raises methylmalonic acid, which is normal here.
Ribonucleotide reductase does not use folate. It is the enzyme blocked by hydroxyurea.
UMP synthase works in pyrimidine synthesis without folate. Its deficiency causes hereditary orotic aciduria.

questions.stem: She is treated with oral folic acid. Five days later, her reticulocyte count is 7%. On a smear stained with new methylene blue, these cells contain a fine blue reticular network. Which of the following does this network represent?
options: Denatured hemoglobin precipitates
Nuclear fragments of DNA
Aggregated iron in mitochondria
Residual ribosomal RNA
approach: A reticulocyte is a young red cell that has just extruded its nucleus.
It still holds ribosomal RNA for a day or two, which supravital dyes precipitate as a network.
A rising count days after folate shows the marrow is now producing red cells.
questions.why: During erythroid maturation the nucleus condenses and is extruded, but the young cell keeps ribosomes that finish hemoglobin synthesis. Supravital dyes such as new methylene blue precipitate this ribosomal RNA into a blue mesh, which defines the reticulocyte. The RNA is lost over about a day in the circulation. A brisk reticulocytosis about 5 to 7 days after folate replacement shows that the marrow can respond once DNA synthesis is restored.
whyNot: Denatured hemoglobin forms Heinz bodies, seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidant stress.
Nuclear DNA remnants are Howell-Jolly bodies, seen after splenectomy or in megaloblastic anemia, as single round dots.
Iron in mitochondria around the nucleus gives ringed sideroblasts in marrow precursors, shown with Prussian blue.
Correct.

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspirate stained with Prussian blue also shows ringed sideroblasts, which resolve after she stops drinking and improves her diet. Deficiency of which of the following cofactors most likely impaired the first step of heme synthesis in her erythroid precursors?
options: Thiamine pyrophosphate
Pyridoxal phosphate
Tetrahydrobiopterin
Flavin adenine dinucleotide
approach: Ringed sideroblasts mean iron is in mitochondria but is not being put into heme.
The first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis is ALA synthase in the mitochondria.
ALA synthase uses pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6, which is often low with heavy alcohol use.
questions.why: Heme synthesis begins in the mitochondria, where ALA synthase joins glycine and succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinic acid. This rate-limiting enzyme needs pyridoxal phosphate. Poor diet and alcohol both lower active B6, so less protoporphyrin is made and iron piles up in mitochondria around the nucleus, forming ringed sideroblasts. Heme normally feeds back to repress ALA synthase.
whyNot: Thiamine pyrophosphate serves pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Its deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy, not sideroblasts.
Correct.
Tetrahydrobiopterin is a cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase and catecholamine synthesis, not heme synthesis.
FAD serves dehydrogenases such as succinate dehydrogenase. It is not the cofactor for ALA synthase.

dx: Secondary polycythemia in a heavy smoker with chronic hypoxemic COPD
case: A 61-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the physician because of morning headaches and fatigue. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. He has a ruddy face, a barrel chest, and no splenomegaly. Arterial PaO2 is 52 mm Hg (75 to 100). Hemoglobin concentration is 19.2 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), and hematocrit is 58% (41 to 53). Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. Serum erythropoietin is 38 mU/mL (4 to 27). Testing for JAK2 V617F is negative. The diagnosis is secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxemia.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man who takes hydrochlorothiazide and drinks little water has a hematocrit of 55% (41 to 53). His oxygen saturation, serum erythropoietin concentration, and spleen size are normal. Which of the following findings is most likely in this second man?
options: Increased red cell mass, low erythropoietin
Increased red cell mass, high erythropoietin
Normal red cell mass, high plasma volume
Normal red cell mass, low plasma volume
approach: Hematocrit is a ratio of red cell volume to total blood volume, so it rises if red cells increase or plasma falls.
Normal erythropoietin with a diuretic and poor intake suggests the plasma is contracted.
This is relative polycythemia: red cell mass is normal and plasma volume is low.
questions.why: In relative polycythemia the hematocrit is high only because plasma volume is reduced, as with diuretics or dehydration. The red cell mass is normal, so there is no stimulus or signal for extra erythropoiesis and erythropoietin is normal. The patient in the case has true, absolute polycythemia with increased red cell mass driven by hypoxemia and appropriately high erythropoietin. Polycythemia vera also raises red cell mass, but with low erythropoietin.
whyNot: Increased red cell mass with low erythropoietin fits polycythemia vera, which would also often show splenomegaly and JAK2 V617F.
Increased red cell mass with high erythropoietin fits secondary polycythemia, as in the smoker with hypoxemia, not this man.
A high plasma volume would dilute the red cells and lower the hematocrit.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how his chronic hypoxemia increases erythropoietin production?
options: Sympathetic stimulation of juxtaglomerular cells
HIF stabilization in renal peritubular interstitial cells
A shift of erythropoietin production to adult hepatocytes
Increased erythropoietin secretion by glomerular podocytes
approach: Erythropoietin in adults comes mainly from peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex.
These cells sense oxygen through hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF).
Low oxygen stops HIF breakdown, so HIF turns on the erythropoietin gene.
questions.why: In normal oxygen, prolyl hydroxylases use oxygen to hydroxylate HIF alpha, which then binds the von Hippel-Lindau protein and is degraded. In hypoxemia the hydroxylation slows, HIF alpha is stabilized, and it drives transcription of the erythropoietin gene in renal peritubular interstitial cells. More erythropoietin raises red cell production and the hematocrit. The same cells make little erythropoietin in chronic kidney disease, and erythropoietin is low in polycythemia vera.
whyNot: Juxtaglomerular cells make renin in response to sympathetic input and low perfusion. They are not the erythropoietin source.
Correct.
Hepatocytes are the main erythropoietin source in the fetus. In adults they add only a small share.
Podocytes form the filtration barrier and do not secrete erythropoietin.

questions.stem: Before bronchoscopy, his throat is sprayed with benzocaine. Twenty minutes later he is cyanotic, and his blood is chocolate brown. Pulse oximetry reads 85%, and his arterial PaO2 is 92 mm Hg on supplemental oxygen. Which of the following best explains his reduced oxygen delivery to tissues?
options: Ferric heme iron, with a left shift of the curve
Ferrous heme iron, with a right shift of the curve
Ferric heme iron, with a right shift of the curve
Ferrous heme iron occupied by carbon monoxide
approach: Chocolate brown blood and cyanosis with a normal PaO2 after benzocaine suggest methemoglobinemia.
Benzocaine oxidizes heme iron from the ferrous (Fe2+) to the ferric (Fe3+) state, which cannot carry oxygen.
The remaining ferrous hemes in each tetramer bind oxygen more tightly, shifting the curve left.
questions.why: Methemoglobin contains ferric iron, which cannot bind oxygen, so oxygen content falls even though PaO2, the dissolved oxygen, is normal. In a partly oxidized tetramer the remaining ferrous hemes hold oxygen more tightly, a left shift that further limits unloading in tissues. Topical anesthetics such as benzocaine, plus nitrites and dapsone, are classic acquired causes. Congenital cases come from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency.
whyNot: Correct.
Normal hemoglobin carries ferrous iron. A right shift would help oxygen unloading rather than impair it.
The iron is ferric, but the shift is to the left. The remaining hemes bind oxygen more tightly.
Carbon monoxide poisoning gives cherry red, not chocolate brown, blood and is not caused by benzocaine.

questions.stem: At a hematocrit of 58%, his erythrocytes, about 7.5 µm in diameter, must still pass through capillaries narrower than themselves. Which of the following features of the mature erythrocyte best allows this?
options: No mitochondria, so no oxygen is consumed
Abundant carbonic anhydrase in the cytosol
Biconcave disc with extra membrane for its volume
Band 3 exchange of bicarbonate for chloride ions in the membrane
approach: Passing through a narrow capillary needs deformability, not a gas transport feature.
A biconcave disc has more surface membrane than a sphere of the same volume.
That surplus membrane lets the cell fold without stretching or rupturing.
questions.why: The biconcave shape gives the red cell a large surface area for its volume. This lets the cell bend and fold to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself and through the slits between splenic cords and sinuses, and it shortens the distance gases must diffuse. When surface area is lost, as in spherocytes, the cell becomes rigid and is trapped in the spleen. The other features help gas transport but not passage through small vessels.
whyNot: Lacking mitochondria means the cell does not use the oxygen it carries. It does not make the cell deformable.
Carbonic anhydrase converts carbon dioxide to bicarbonate for carbon dioxide transport. It does not affect cell shape.
Correct.
Band 3 carries out the chloride shift for carbon dioxide transport. It also anchors the cytoskeleton, but the exchange itself does not allow passage.

topics: Red cell features for gas transport

dx: Hemoglobin H disease from deletion of three alpha globin genes
case: A 27-year-old woman whose parents emigrated from Thailand comes to the physician because of lifelong fatigue and intermittent yellow eyes. She has scleral icterus, and the spleen tip is palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.1 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), MCV is 61 fL (80 to 100), and reticulocyte count is 6% (0.5 to 2.5). Serum ferritin is normal. Supravital staining with brilliant cresyl blue shows many red cells with fine, evenly spaced inclusions. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows 12% hemoglobin H. Genetic testing shows deletion of three of her four alpha globin genes (--/-α). The diagnosis is hemoglobin H disease.

questions.stem: Her husband has mild microcytosis with a normal hemoglobin concentration. Genetic testing shows that he lacks both alpha globin genes on one chromosome 16 (--/αα). What is the probability that any one of their pregnancies will result in hydrops fetalis with hemoglobin Barts?
approach: List each parent's possible gametes: she passes either (--) or (-α); he passes either (--) or (αα).
Hydrops fetalis requires a fetus with no alpha genes (--/--).
That needs (--) from each parent: 1/2 times 1/2 equals 1/4.
questions.why: Each parent passes one chromosome 16 at random. She gives (--) half the time, and her husband gives (--) half the time, so one pregnancy in four is (--/--), with no alpha chains. Gamma chains then form tetramers (hemoglobin Barts) that bind oxygen too tightly to release it, causing hydrops fetalis. The same couple has a 1/4 chance of a child with HbH disease (--/-α), 1/4 of trait (--/αα), and 1/4 of a silent carrier (-α/αα). Cis deletions (--) are common in Southeast Asia, which is why hydrops fetalis is seen mainly there.
whyNot: A zero risk would apply if either parent had at least one alpha gene on each chromosome, as in trans trait (-α/-α).
Correct.
50% is the chance that a child inherits her (--) chromosome, but hydrops also requires (--) from the father.
75% is the chance that a child has at least one (--) chromosome, not two.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin H is a tetramer of four beta globin chains. Which of the following best explains why it delivers little oxygen to her tissues?
options: Low oxygen affinity with strong cooperativity
Normal affinity with an exaggerated Bohr effect
Very high oxygen affinity with no cooperativity
Low affinity from tight binding of 2,3-BPG
approach: Normal oxygen unloading needs alpha-beta subunit contacts that allow the shift between tense and relaxed states.
A tetramer of identical beta chains cannot make that shift, so it stays in a high affinity form.
High affinity with no cooperativity gives a hyperbolic curve that releases little oxygen at tissue PO2.
questions.why: Cooperative binding in hemoglobin A depends on the interface between alpha and beta subunits, which lets the molecule switch from the tense to the relaxed state. Beta4 tetramers lack this interface, so they behave like myoglobin, with a hyperbolic curve, very high oxygen affinity, and no Bohr effect. They hold oxygen at tissue PO2 and give little to cells. HbH is also unstable and precipitates as inclusions, which shortens red cell survival.
whyNot: Low affinity would help unloading, and HbH has no cooperativity.
HbH has no Bohr effect, because it lacks the alpha-beta contacts that the Bohr effect needs.
Correct.
2,3-BPG lowers affinity by binding the tense, deoxy form of hemoglobin A. HbH cannot shift into that tense form, so 2,3-BPG does not lower its high affinity.

questions.stem: Her erythrocytes survive for much less than the normal 120 days. Which of the following best describes where and how most of her erythrocytes are removed?
options: Trapped in splenic cords and engulfed by macrophages
Lysed by complement within the circulating blood
Destroyed by marrow macrophages before ever being released
Cleared by hepatic Kupffer cells after IgG coating
approach: Normal aged red cells become rigid and are removed by macrophages, mainly in the spleen.
HbH inclusions make her cells rigid much earlier.
Rigid cells cannot pass from the splenic cords into the sinuses, so red pulp macrophages engulf them, which also enlarges the spleen.
questions.why: Red cells have no nucleus or ribosomes, so they cannot replace worn enzymes and membrane proteins. After about 120 days they lose deformability and are caught in the splenic cords of the red pulp, where macrophages phagocytose them, with the liver as a backup. Precipitated HbH damages her cell membranes, so this same extravascular removal happens after a much shorter life. The constant work enlarges her spleen.
whyNot: Correct.
Complement lysis in the blood is intravascular hemolysis, as in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria or ABO transfusion reactions.
Destruction of precursors in the marrow is ineffective erythropoiesis, the dominant process in beta thalassemia major rather than in HbH disease.
IgG coating with clearance is antibody-mediated hemolysis, and there is no antibody here. IgG-coated cells are cleared mainly in the spleen.

topics: Red cell life span and removal

questions.stem: On her Wright-stained peripheral blood smear, which of the following provides the best internal size reference for judging that her erythrocytes are microcytic?
options: Diameter of a platelet
Diameter of a segmented neutrophil
Diameter of a monocyte
Nucleus of a small lymphocyte
approach: A normal red cell is about 7 to 8 µm across.
Find a cell on the same smear with a structure of about that size.
The round nucleus of a small mature lymphocyte is about the size of a normal red cell.
questions.why: A small lymphocyte has a dense, round nucleus about 7 to 8 µm wide with a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm. A normal red cell is about the same diameter, so red cells clearly smaller than that nucleus are microcytic. Platelets are much smaller, and neutrophils and monocytes are much larger, so they are poor references.
whyNot: Platelets are about 2 to 3 µm across and vary in size, so they do not help judge red cell size.
A segmented neutrophil is about 12 to 15 µm across, well above normal red cell size.
A monocyte is the largest normal blood cell, about 15 to 20 µm, with a folded nucleus.
Correct.

topics: Normal blood cells on a smear

dx: ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn in a group A infant of a group O mother
case: A 30-hour-old boy born at term is evaluated for jaundice that began at 20 hours of age. This is his mother's first pregnancy. She is blood group O, Rh-positive, and received no transfusions. The infant is group A, Rh-positive. He is feeding well. His sclerae and skin to the chest are yellow, and the liver and spleen are each palpable 2 cm below the costal margins. Hemoglobin concentration is 13.5 g/dL (14.5 to 22.5), and reticulocyte count is 9% (3 to 7). Total serum bilirubin is 13.8 mg/dL, above the phototherapy threshold for his age, with direct bilirubin of 0.4 mg/dL. The smear shows many spherocytes. The diagnosis is ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this disorder occurred during the mother's first pregnancy?
options: Group O adults make IgG anti-A without red cell exposure
Fetal red cells entered her blood during the first trimester
Naturally occurring IgM anti-A crossed the placenta
Rh-positive fetal cells sensitized her during labor
approach: ABO antibodies form in early life without transfusion or pregnancy, after exposure to A-like and B-like antigens on gut bacteria.
Only IgG crosses the placenta.
Group O people often make IgG anti-A and anti-B, so no prior pregnancy is needed.
questions.why: Anti-A and anti-B are naturally occurring, made in infancy in response to similar carbohydrate antigens on gut bacteria and food. In group A and group B people they are mostly IgM, which cannot cross the placenta. Group O people make a large share of IgG anti-A and anti-B, which crosses the placenta and coats fetal group A or B cells. ABO disease is usually mild because fetal A and B antigens are weakly developed and are also found on other tissues that absorb the antibody.
whyNot: Correct.
Sensitization from fetal cells is the mechanism of anti-D disease, which usually spares a first pregnancy. ABO antibodies do not need it.
IgM is a large pentamer that does not cross the placenta.
The mother is Rh-positive, so she cannot be sensitized to the D antigen.

questions.stem: A direct antiglobulin test is done on the infant's red cells. The mother's serum is tested with an indirect antiglobulin antibody screen that uses group O reagent red cells. Which of the following pairs of results is most likely?
options: Infant direct test negative; maternal screen positive
Infant direct test strongly positive; maternal screen positive
Infant direct test negative; maternal screen negative
Infant direct test weakly positive; maternal screen negative
approach: The direct test detects antibody already on the infant's red cells; in ABO disease little IgG binds, so it is often only weakly positive.
The indirect screen detects maternal antibodies against non-ABO red cell antigens.
Group O reagent cells lack A and B antigens, so the mother's anti-A does not react and the screen is negative.
questions.why: In ABO hemolytic disease, small amounts of maternal IgG anti-A coat the infant's cells, so the direct antiglobulin test is usually weakly positive. The mother's antibody screen uses group O cells so that it detects only clinically important non-ABO alloantibodies, such as anti-D. Her anti-A therefore does not show up. After birth the placenta no longer clears bilirubin, and the rising unconjugated bilirubin must be watched because of the risk of kernicterus.
whyNot: A positive maternal screen with a negative infant test suggests a maternal alloantibody that the infant's cells lack.
A strongly positive infant test with a positive maternal screen fits anti-D disease, not ABO disease.

The direct test is sometimes negative in ABO disease, but with hemolysis this brisk a weak positive is more likely. Two negative tests would also fit a non-immune cause such as hereditary spherocytosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: His end-tidal carbon monoxide concentration, corrected for ambient levels, is increased. Which of the following reactions produced this carbon monoxide?
options: Reduction of biliverdin to bilirubin
Conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid
Opening of the heme ring by heme oxygenase
Bacterial conversion of bilirubin to urobilinogen
approach: Hemolysis releases heme, which macrophages break down.
Heme oxygenase opens the heme ring, giving biliverdin, free iron, and one carbon monoxide molecule per heme.
Exhaled carbon monoxide therefore rises in proportion to heme breakdown.
questions.why: In macrophages, heme oxygenase cleaves the porphyrin ring of heme, releasing ferrous iron and carbon monoxide and forming biliverdin. Biliverdin reductase then makes unconjugated bilirubin, which travels on albumin to the liver for conjugation by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase. Because each heme gives one carbon monoxide, an increased end-tidal carbon monoxide shows increased heme breakdown, here from hemolysis.
whyNot: Biliverdin reductase uses NADPH to make bilirubin and releases no carbon monoxide.
Glucuronidation in hepatocytes makes bilirubin water soluble and releases no carbon monoxide.
Correct.
Gut bacteria convert conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen in the colon, a step that releases no carbon monoxide.

questions.stem: His liver and spleen are enlarged partly because of extramedullary erythropoiesis in organs that made blood before birth. At 14 weeks' gestation, which of the following was the main site of his red cell production?
options: Yolk sac blood islands
Fetal liver
Long bone marrow
Fetal thymus
approach: Recall the order of blood-forming sites: yolk sac first, then liver (with some spleen), then bone marrow.
The yolk sac works from about week 3 to week 8.
The liver dominates from about week 6 until bone marrow takes over in the third trimester.
questions.why: Blood formation starts in yolk sac blood islands in week 3. By about week 6 the liver becomes the main site and stays so through midgestation, with a smaller role for the spleen. Bone marrow takes over gradually and becomes the main site late in pregnancy. Because the liver and spleen kept this ability, they can resume making blood when demand is high, as with hemolysis.
whyNot: Yolk sac blood islands make primitive red cells only in the first weeks, ending by about week 8.
Correct.
Bone marrow becomes the main site only in the third trimester.
The thymus is where T cells mature. It is not a main site of red cell production.

dx: Meningococcal sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome after splenectomy
case: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 10 hours after the onset of fever, headache, and a spreading rash. She had a splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision at age 15. Temperature is 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg. She has petechiae and large purpuric patches on the trunk and legs and oozes blood from venipuncture sites. Platelet count is 38,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), PT is 24 seconds (11 to 13.5), PTT is 58 seconds (25 to 35), fibrinogen is 90 mg/dL (200 to 400), and D-dimer is markedly increased. The smear shows schistocytes. Blood cultures grow gram-negative diplococci. The diagnosis is meningococcal sepsis with DIC.

questions.stem: Despite fluids and vasopressors, her hypotension persists. Serum sodium is 128 mEq/L (136 to 145), and serum potassium is 5.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0). CT shows bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Loss of hormones from which of the following parts of the adrenal glands best explains these findings?
options: Chromaffin cells of the medulla
Zona reticularis of the cortex
Glomerulosa and fasciculata of the cortex
Zona fasciculata only, sparing the zona glomerulosa
approach: Microthrombi in DIC cause hemorrhagic necrosis of both adrenal glands (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome).
Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia point to loss of aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa.
Pressor-resistant shock points to loss of cortisol from the zona fasciculata.
questions.why: In DIC, fibrin microthrombi block small vessels in many organs. In the adrenals this causes hemorrhagic necrosis of the cortex, so both aldosterone and cortisol are lost at once. Without aldosterone the kidney wastes sodium and retains potassium. Without cortisol, vessels respond poorly to catecholamines, so shock does not respond to vasopressors. The rich arterial supply of the adrenal, draining into a single central vein, favors hemorrhage.
whyNot: Loss of medullary epinephrine is covered by the sympathetic nervous system and does not cause adrenal crisis or hyperkalemia.
The zona reticularis makes adrenal androgens, whose loss causes no acute crisis.
Correct.
Loss of cortisol alone can cause hypotension and hyponatremia, but hyperkalemia requires loss of aldosterone from the glomerulosa.

questions.stem: Which of the following most directly initiates the coagulation in this patient's disseminated intravascular coagulation?
options: Tissue factor expressed by monocytes and endothelium
Bacterial coagulase converting prothrombin to thrombin
Bacterial protease cleaving fibrinogen to fibrin
Antibody-coated platelets aggregating in small vessels
approach: Sepsis is one of the most common triggers of DIC.
Neisseria meningitidis sheds lipooligosaccharide (endotoxin) in large amounts.
Endotoxin and the cytokines it induces make monocytes and endothelial cells express tissue factor, which starts coagulation through factor VII.
questions.why: Meningococcal lipooligosaccharide acts as a potent endotoxin. It and the cytokines it induces (TNF, IL-1) cause monocytes and endothelial cells to express tissue factor, which activates factor VII and drives widespread thrombin generation. At the same time endothelial anticoagulant pathways are suppressed. Clotting factors and platelets are consumed, giving prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia, high D-dimer, and schistocytes.
whyNot: Correct.
Coagulase is made by Staphylococcus aureus, not Neisseria meningitidis.
Some snake venoms act this way, but meningococci do not make a fibrinogen-cleaving protease.
Antibody-coated platelets are destroyed in immune thrombocytopenia. That process does not start coagulation.

questions.stem: Her purpura fulminans reflects microvascular thrombosis worsened by loss of endothelial thrombomodulin during sepsis. Normally, thrombomodulin limits clotting by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Accelerating antithrombin inactivation of factor Xa
Binding thrombin so that it activates protein C
Converting plasminogen to plasmin on fibrin
Blocking the tissue factor and factor VIIa complex
approach: Thrombomodulin is an endothelial receptor for thrombin.
Bound thrombin stops cleaving fibrinogen and instead activates protein C.
Activated protein C, with protein S, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
questions.why: When thrombin binds thrombomodulin on intact endothelium, it switches from a procoagulant to an anticoagulant enzyme and activates protein C. Activated protein C, helped by protein S, cleaves factors Va and VIIIa and slows further thrombin formation. Sepsis cytokines lower thrombomodulin and consume protein C, so small vessel clotting runs unchecked and skin infarcts appear as purpura fulminans.
whyNot: Heparan sulfate on endothelium, and heparin as a drug, speed antithrombin inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa.
Correct.
Tissue plasminogen activator converts plasminogen to plasmin on fibrin.
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor blocks the tissue factor and factor VIIa complex after it has made some factor Xa.

questions.stem: She had not received the meningococcal conjugate vaccine before her splenectomy. Which of the following best explains why that vaccine would have protected her?
options: Capsule-specific IgM made without T cell help
Cytotoxic T cells that lyse infected host cells
Neutralizing IgA that blocks endotoxin in plasma
T cell dependent IgG that opsonizes the capsule
approach: Encapsulated bacteria resist phagocytosis unless antibody and complement coat the capsule.
The spleen normally clears these bacteria quickly with natural IgM, marginal zone B cells, and macrophages.
A conjugate vaccine links the capsule to a protein so helper T cells drive class switching to IgG and memory, which opsonizes bacteria for clearance elsewhere.
questions.why: Capsular polysaccharide alone gives a T cell independent response with mostly IgM and little memory, a response that relies heavily on the spleen. Linking the polysaccharide to a carrier protein recruits helper T cells, which drive class switching to high-affinity IgG and memory B cells. IgG and complement on the capsule allow killing and clearance by liver macrophages and neutrophils, so asplenic patients are protected. Vaccines are ideally given at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy.
whyNot: IgM made without T cell help is the response to plain polysaccharide vaccines. It is weak, short lived, and depends on the spleen.
Neisseria meningitidis is an extracellular pathogen, so cytotoxic T cells give little protection.
IgA acts mainly at mucosal surfaces. It does not neutralize endotoxin in plasma.
Correct.

case: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of right groin and lower abdominal pain that began 2 days after he fell from his bicycle. He has had several knee hemarthroses since early childhood, and his maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. He holds his right hip flexed, and passive extension causes severe pain. Sensation is decreased over the anterior thigh. Platelet count is 260,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), PT is 12 seconds (11 to 13.5), and PTT is 68 seconds (25 to 35). Factor IX activity is 2% (50 to 150). Ultrasonography shows a right iliopsoas hematoma. The diagnosis is hemophilia B.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with no previous bleeding history develops large bruises and a thigh hematoma. Her PT and platelet count are normal, and her PTT is 71 seconds (25 to 35). A 1:1 mix with normal plasma corrects the PTT at first, but it prolongs again after 2 hours of incubation at 37 °C (98.6 °F). Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
options: Lupus anticoagulant
Autoantibody against factor VIII
Heterozygous carrier of hemophilia B
Vitamin K deficiency
approach: An isolated prolonged PTT with bleeding points to a problem with factor VIII, IX, or XI.
A factor deficiency corrects on mixing and stays corrected; an inhibitor does not stay corrected.
Correction that is lost after incubation is typical of a time-dependent factor VIII autoantibody.
questions.why: In hemophilia A or B, normal plasma supplies the missing factor, so the PTT corrects on mixing and stays normal. Acquired factor VIII inhibitors are IgG autoantibodies, often in older adults or after childbirth. They work slowly, so the mix corrects at first and then prolongs again after incubation. New bleeding late in life with no family history also argues against an inherited disorder.
whyNot: Lupus anticoagulant usually fails to correct even at once, and it causes clotting rather than bleeding.
Correct.
A carrier with low factor IX would correct on mixing and stay corrected, and bleeding would not start at age 72.
Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT first because factor VII has the shortest half-life.

questions.stem: As an adult, he has children with a woman who has no personal or family history of a bleeding disorder. What is the probability, expressed as a proportion, that any one of their daughters will be a carrier of hemophilia B?
approach: Hemophilia B is X-linked recessive; the factor IX gene is on the X chromosome.
An affected father passes his only X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son.
Every daughter is therefore a carrier, and no son is affected.
questions.why: Hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive. A father gives his X chromosome to all daughters, so each daughter receives his mutant factor IX gene and is an obligate carrier. Sons receive his Y chromosome and a normal X from their mother, so they are unaffected. Carriers usually have about half-normal factor IX, and some have mild bleeding.
whyNot: A zero risk would apply to his sons, who inherit his Y chromosome.
25% is the chance that any child of a carrier mother and unaffected father is an affected son.
50% is the chance that a daughter of a carrier mother and unaffected father is a carrier.
Correct.

questions.stem: At presentation, his hemoglobin concentration is 12.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5). He receives factor IX concentrate and no transfusion. Repeat ultrasonography 36 hours later shows no growth of the hematoma, but his hemoglobin concentration is now 9.8 g/dL. Which of the following best explains this fall?
options: Movement of interstitial fluid into the plasma
Delayed fall in erythropoietin output
Iron deficiency from the earlier blood loss
Splenic sequestration of circulating red cells
approach: Acute bleeding removes red cells and plasma together, so the first hemoglobin is near the starting value.
Over the next 1 to 2 days, fluid moves from the interstitium into the vessels to restore volume.
This dilutes the remaining red cells, so hemoglobin falls even though bleeding has stopped.
questions.why: Whole blood lost in a hemorrhage has the same hemoglobin concentration as the blood left behind, so the first value underestimates the loss. Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure then draws interstitial fluid into the plasma, and the kidney retains salt and water. This restores volume over 24 to 72 hours and dilutes the remaining red cells, revealing the true anemia. Reticulocytes rise a few days later, and iron deficiency develops only with repeated or chronic loss.
whyNot: Correct.
Erythropoietin rises, not falls, after blood loss. Its effect on the count takes days and would raise hemoglobin.
Iron deficiency develops over weeks of repeated loss, not within 36 hours.
Splenic sequestration occurs in sickle cell disease and portal hypertension. Nothing here suggests it.

questions.stem: His tissue factor pathway is intact, yet he bleeds into deep muscles after minor trauma. Which of the following best explains why tissue factor alone cannot sustain clotting at his injury site?
options: Factor VIIa needs factor IXa as its cofactor to activate X
Tissue factor works only through factor XII and the contact pathway
TF-VIIa is soon blocked by TFPI, so IXa-VIIIa must make Xa
Thrombin is made only when factor XI is activated by factor IXa
approach: Tissue factor and factor VIIa start clotting by making a small amount of factor Xa and factor IXa.
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) quickly shuts down that complex once some Xa forms.
Ongoing Xa production then depends on the IXa-VIIIa complex on platelets, which he cannot form.
questions.why: Tissue factor with factor VIIa makes a little thrombin to start clotting, but tissue factor pathway inhibitor, bound to factor Xa, soon blocks this complex. Sustained thrombin generation then depends on the intrinsic tenase, factor IXa with its cofactor VIIIa on activated platelet surfaces, which makes most of the factor Xa. Without factor IX this amplification fails, so clots are weak and bleeding continues into joints and muscles even though the PT is normal.
whyNot: Factor VIIa uses tissue factor as its cofactor. Factor VIIIa is the cofactor for factor IXa.
Tissue factor activates factor VII, not factor XII. The contact pathway starts with factor XII.
Correct.
The order is reversed: factor XIa activates factor IX, and thrombin also activates factor XI.

dx: Immune thrombocytopenia in a young woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibodies
case: A 29-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the physician because of bleeding gums and a rash on her legs for 1 week. She has had two pregnancy losses at 18 and 21 weeks' gestation. She has scattered petechiae on the shins and no splenomegaly. Platelet count is 18,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). Hemoglobin concentration and leukocyte count are normal. The smear shows large platelets and no schistocytes. PT is normal, and PTT is 46 seconds (25 to 35) and does not correct on mixing. Anticardiolipin and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies are positive. A bone marrow biopsy shows increased megakaryocytes. The diagnosis is immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) secondary to lupus, with antiphospholipid antibodies.

questions.stem: Her platelet count has stayed below 50,000/mm3 for 14 months. Which of the following features best distinguishes her disease from acute ITP in a 4-year-old after a viral infection?
options: Increased megakaryocytes in the marrow
Isolated thrombocytopenia on the blood count
IgG antibodies against platelet GpIIb/IIIa
Little chance of spontaneous remission
approach: List what childhood and adult ITP share: antiplatelet IgG, splenic clearance, isolated thrombocytopenia, and increased marrow megakaryocytes.
Then find what differs: onset, course, and outcome.
Chronic adult ITP, often linked to lupus, rarely resolves on its own, while childhood ITP usually resolves within weeks to months.
questions.why: In both forms, IgG autoantibodies, often against GpIIb/IIIa, coat platelets, which splenic macrophages then remove. The marrow responds with more megakaryocytes, and the blood shows only low platelets. Acute childhood ITP follows a viral infection, starts suddenly, and resolves on its own in most children. Chronic adult ITP is more common in women of childbearing age, may be secondary to lupus, and seldom remits without treatment.
whyNot: Increased marrow megakaryocytes are seen in both forms because platelet destruction is peripheral.
Isolated thrombocytopenia is seen in both forms and helps separate ITP from marrow failure, not acute from chronic ITP.
Antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa occur in both childhood and adult ITP.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man in the same clinic has Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia and a new hemolytic anemia, with bluish fingertips in the cold. His direct antiglobulin test is positive with anti-C3 reagent and negative with anti-IgG reagent. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Warm IgG that dissociates once complement binds
Cold IgM that fixes C3, then detaches on warming
IgE against the red cell I antigen on mast cells
Drug-induced IgG bound to red cell membrane proteins
approach: Mycoplasma infection with cold-induced symptoms suggests cold agglutinin disease.
The cold antibody is IgM against the I antigen, binding in cooler fingers and toes.
IgM fixes complement and then falls off at body temperature, so only C3 remains on the red cells.
questions.why: Mycoplasma pneumoniae can induce IgM antibodies against the I antigen. These bind red cells in cool peripheral vessels, cause agglutination and acrocyanosis, and fix complement. When the cells warm in the core circulation, the IgM detaches but C3 stays on the membrane, so the direct antiglobulin test shows C3 only. C3-coated cells are cleared mainly by liver macrophages. Warm autoimmune hemolysis, as with lupus, is IgG-mediated and gives spherocytes.
whyNot: Warm IgG antibodies stay bound at body temperature, so the anti-IgG reagent would be positive.
Correct.
IgE does not mediate autoimmune hemolysis, and mast cell activation causes allergy, not red cell destruction.
Drug-induced IgG would give a positive anti-IgG result, and he has no drug exposure described.

topics: Warm versus cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia

questions.stem: She is started on a drug that activates the receptor for the main hormone regulating megakaryocyte growth and platelet production. Which of the following describes that hormone and its main source?
options: Erythropoietin from renal peritubular cells
Interleukin-5 from helper T cells
Thrombopoietin from hepatocytes
G-CSF from marrow stromal cells and macrophages
approach: Match each lineage to its main growth factor.
Megakaryocytes and platelets are driven by thrombopoietin, which acts on the MPL receptor.
Thrombopoietin is made mostly by the liver at a fairly constant rate.
questions.why: Thrombopoietin is made mainly by hepatocytes. It binds the MPL receptor on megakaryocytes and their progenitors to increase their number, size, and platelet output. Circulating platelets bind and clear thrombopoietin, so free levels rise when platelet mass falls. Drugs that activate the thrombopoietin receptor raise platelet counts in chronic ITP.
whyNot: Erythropoietin from renal peritubular cells drives red cell production.
Interleukin-5 from Th2 cells drives eosinophil production.
Correct.
G-CSF drives neutrophil production.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her two second-trimester pregnancy losses?
options: Placental thrombosis from antiphospholipid antibodies
Fetal thrombocytopenia from maternal antiplatelet IgG
Anti-dsDNA immune complexes in the fetal kidneys
Bleeding from the prolonged partial thromboplastin time
approach: Recurrent pregnancy loss in a woman with lupus and positive anticardiolipin and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies suggests antiphospholipid syndrome.
The prolonged PTT is a laboratory effect: the antibodies bind phospholipid in the test tube.
In the body they promote clotting, including in placental vessels.
questions.why: Antiphospholipid antibodies bind phospholipid-protein complexes such as beta2 glycoprotein I on endothelial cells, platelets, monocytes, and trophoblast. This activates these cells and complement and makes them procoagulant. In the placenta the result is thrombosis, infarction, and poor trophoblast function, which cause fetal loss. In vitro the same antibodies tie up the phospholipid in the PTT reagent, so the PTT is prolonged even though the patient tends to clot.
whyNot: Correct.
Maternal antiplatelet IgG can cross the placenta and lower the fetal platelet count, but this rarely causes fetal death.
Anti-dsDNA immune complexes damage the mother's kidneys in lupus nephritis, not the fetal kidneys.
The prolonged PTT is an in vitro artifact of the antibodies. It does not cause bleeding.

dx: Acquired von Willebrand syndrome from severe aortic stenosis with angiodysplasia bleeding (Heyde syndrome)
case: A 78-year-old man comes to the physician because of black stools on and off for 6 months and shortness of breath on exertion. He fainted once while climbing stairs. He takes low-dose aspirin. A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border. Echocardiography shows severe aortic stenosis. Colonoscopy shows several angiodysplasias in the cecum and ascending colon. Hemoglobin concentration is 8.4 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), MCV is 72 fL (80 to 100), and serum ferritin is 8 ng/mL (24 to 336). Platelet count and PT are normal. Von Willebrand factor multimer analysis shows loss of the highest molecular weight multimers. The diagnosis is acquired von Willebrand syndrome from aortic stenosis with angiodysplasia bleeding (Heyde syndrome).

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the loss of the largest von Willebrand factor multimers in his plasma?
options: Shear stress unfolding them for ADAMTS13 cleavage
Autoantibodies speeding clearance of the multimers
Reduced synthesis by endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies
Consumption of the multimers on angiodysplastic vessels
approach: Blood flow through a narrow aortic valve creates very high shear stress.
High shear stretches the largest von Willebrand factor multimers and exposes the site that ADAMTS13 cuts.
The largest multimers are the best at capturing platelets, so their loss impairs platelet adhesion in fast-flowing vessels.
questions.why: Von Willebrand factor bridges exposed subendothelial collagen to platelet GpIb, and the largest multimers do this best under high shear. In severe aortic stenosis, turbulent flow unfolds these multimers so ADAMTS13 cleaves them, leaving a pattern like type 2A von Willebrand disease. Platelets adhere poorly, so fragile angiodysplasias bleed. The defect often improves after valve replacement.
whyNot: Correct.
Autoantibodies cause acquired von Willebrand syndrome in some lymphoproliferative and autoimmune disorders, but the shear mechanism fits aortic stenosis.
Synthesis and storage are normal here. Endothelial cells keep making and releasing large multimers.
Angiodysplasias are the bleeding sites, not the cause of the multimer loss.

topics: Von Willebrand factor multimers and ADAMTS13

questions.stem: Two years ago, before his anemia developed, his blood counts were normal. As slow intestinal bleeding depleted his iron stores, which of the following laboratory changes most likely appeared first?
options: Increased red cell distribution width
Decreased mean corpuscular volume
Decreased serum ferritin
Decreased hemoglobin concentration
approach: Chronic blood loss drains storage iron before it limits red cell production.
Serum ferritin reflects storage iron, so it falls first.
Only after stores are empty do RDW rise, MCV fall, and hemoglobin drop.
questions.why: Iron deficiency develops in stages. First, storage iron in macrophages and hepatocytes is used up, which lowers serum ferritin while hemoglobin is still normal. Next, serum iron and transferrin saturation fall and TIBC rises. Then iron-deficient erythropoiesis produces small cells of mixed sizes, raising the RDW and lowering the MCV, and finally microcytic hypochromic anemia appears.
whyNot: The RDW rises once new small cells mix with older normal cells, after stores are gone.
The MCV falls only after many iron-deficient cells have entered the blood.
Correct.
Anemia is the last stage, after stores are empty and red cell production is limited.

questions.stem: A bone marrow biopsy shows very large cells with multilobed nuclei and abundant granular cytoplasm lying against the sinusoid walls. Which of the following best describes how these cells supply platelets to the blood?
options: Mitotic division into small anucleate daughter cells
Budding of granule-filled vesicles from their nuclei
Repeated mitosis without cytokinesis in the circulation
Proplatelet extensions that fragment into sinusoids
approach: The large multilobed cells are megakaryocytes, which become polyploid by replicating DNA without dividing.
They extend long cytoplasmic processes (proplatelets) through the sinusoid wall.
Blood flow breaks these processes into platelets, which carry granules but no nucleus.
questions.why: Megakaryocytes undergo endomitosis, copying DNA without cell division, to become large polyploid cells. Each one pushes proplatelet processes into the marrow sinusoids, where they fragment into thousands of platelets. Platelets carry alpha granules (von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen) and dense granules (ADP, calcium, serotonin) but no nucleus. Because they cannot make new proteins, aspirin blocks their cyclooxygenase for their whole life of about 7 to 10 days.
whyNot: Megakaryocytes do not divide into platelets. Platelets are cytoplasmic fragments, not daughter cells.
Platelet granules form in the cytoplasm and are carried in cytoplasmic fragments, not budded from the nucleus.
Endomitosis occurs in the marrow as megakaryocytes mature. It does not happen in the circulation.
Correct.

questions.stem: His low-dose aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase-1. Loss of which of the following platelet functions results most directly from this inhibition?
options: Adhesion to von Willebrand factor through GpIb
Thromboxane-driven vasoconstriction and recruitment
Fibrinogen binding to glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors
Release of von Willebrand factor from alpha granules
approach: Cyclooxygenase-1 turns arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2, which platelets convert to thromboxane A2.
Thromboxane A2 constricts vessels and activates more platelets.
Aspirin therefore weakens the amplification step of primary hemostasis, not the first adhesion.
questions.why: Primary hemostasis begins with vasoconstriction and adhesion of platelets to von Willebrand factor through GpIb. Adherent platelets then release ADP and make thromboxane A2, which constricts vessels and recruits more platelets. Fibrinogen then links activated GpIIb/IIIa receptors to form the platelet plug. Aspirin blocks thromboxane A2 synthesis, which weakens recruitment and adds to his bleeding from angiodysplasias.
whyNot: Adhesion through GpIb does not need cyclooxygenase. It is lost in Bernard-Soulier syndrome and von Willebrand disease.
Correct.
GpIIb/IIIa activation is reduced only indirectly. It is blocked directly in Glanzmann thrombasthenia and by GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors.
Alpha granule release is triggered by several agonists, including thrombin, and does not depend mainly on cyclooxygenase.

dx: Vitamin K deficiency coagulopathy from fat malabsorption in celiac disease
case: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. For 2 years she has had bloating, chronic diarrhea with bulky, foul-smelling stools, and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. She has several ecchymoses on the arms. Serum IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are positive, and a duodenal biopsy specimen shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Hemoglobin concentration is 10.1 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), and MCV is 74 fL (80 to 100). Platelet count is 290,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), PT is 22 seconds (11 to 13.5), PTT is 41 seconds (25 to 35), and fibrinogen is 310 mg/dL (200 to 400). The diagnosis is vitamin K deficiency from celiac disease.

questions.stem: Her liver is releasing clotting factors that lack gamma-carboxyglutamate residues. Which of the following anticoagulant proteins is also produced in this undercarboxylated form?
options: Antithrombin
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor
Protein C
Thrombomodulin
approach: Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum.
Its targets are procoagulant factors II, VII, IX, and X and anticoagulant proteins C and S.
Without carboxylation these proteins cannot bind calcium and phospholipid membranes.
questions.why: Gamma-glutamyl carboxylase uses reduced vitamin K to add a carboxyl group to glutamate residues, forming gamma-carboxyglutamate. These residues bind calcium, which lets the proteins attach to phosphatidylserine on activated platelets. Factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S all need this step. Protein C has a short half-life, which is why warfarin, which blocks vitamin K recycling, can briefly cause clotting at the start of therapy.
whyNot: Antithrombin is a serine protease inhibitor made by the liver that does not need vitamin K.
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor is made mostly by endothelium and does not need gamma-carboxylation.
Correct.
Thrombomodulin is an endothelial membrane protein that does not need vitamin K.

questions.stem: She eats leafy green vegetables daily and has taken no antibiotics. Which of the following best explains her vitamin K deficiency?
options: Loss of intrinsic factor from parietal cell injury
Impaired hepatic synthesis of clotting proteins
Overgrowth of bacteria that degrade vitamin K
Poor micellar absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
approach: Vitamin K is fat soluble and is absorbed with dietary fat in bile acid micelles.
Villous atrophy in celiac disease reduces small bowel absorption of fat, as her steatorrhea shows.
Poor fat absorption leads to deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K despite adequate intake.
questions.why: Vitamin K from leafy greens (phylloquinone) is absorbed in the small intestine only when packaged into micelles with fat and bile acids. Celiac disease flattens the villi, so fat and fat-soluble vitamins pass unabsorbed, as her bulky, foul-smelling stools show. Other common causes of deficiency are newborns not given prophylaxis, prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics, and poor intake. The PT prolongs first because factor VII has the shortest half-life.
whyNot: Intrinsic factor is needed for vitamin B12 absorption, not vitamin K.
Her liver can still make the proteins, but without vitamin K they are not carboxylated. Liver failure would also lower fibrinogen.
Gut bacteria make some vitamin K2. Losing them to prolonged antibiotics, not overgrowth, adds to deficiency.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before her biopsy, liver disease was considered as a cause of her prolonged PT. Which of the following results would best favor vitamin K deficiency over liver failure?
options: Low factor VII activity
Normal factor V activity
Normal factor VIII activity
Prolonged prothrombin time
approach: The liver makes almost all clotting factors, but only II, VII, IX, and X need vitamin K.
Factor V is made in the liver without vitamin K.
Normal factor V points to vitamin K deficiency, while low factor V points to failing liver synthesis.
questions.why: Liver failure lowers all hepatic clotting factors, including factor V and fibrinogen, and often causes thrombocytopenia from portal hypertension. Vitamin K deficiency lowers only factors II, VII, IX, and X, so factor V, fibrinogen, and platelets stay normal. Factor VIII is made mainly by endothelial cells, so it is normal or even high in liver disease and normal in vitamin K deficiency. A prolonged PT that corrects within about a day of parenteral vitamin K also supports deficiency.
whyNot: Factor VII has the shortest half-life and falls early in both disorders.
Correct.
Factor VIII is normal in vitamin K deficiency and normal or high in liver disease, so it does not separate them.
The PT is prolonged in both disorders.

topics: Liver failure versus vitamin K deficiency

questions.stem: Her microcytic anemia is caused by iron deficiency, although her diet contains adequate iron. Damage to which of the following sites best explains her poor iron absorption?
options: Duodenal enterocytes expressing DMT1
Terminal ileal enterocytes with cubilin receptors
Gastric parietal cells secreting acid
Colonic epithelium absorbing short-chain fatty acids
approach: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and upper jejunum.
Celiac disease injures the proximal small bowel most.
Loss of the villous enterocytes that take up ferrous iron through DMT1 causes iron deficiency.
questions.why: Dietary nonheme iron is reduced to the ferrous form by duodenal cytochrome b and taken into duodenal enterocytes by DMT1. It leaves the cell through ferroportin, is oxidized, and binds transferrin in plasma, with any excess stored as ferritin. Hepcidin controls this step by degrading ferroportin. Celiac disease damages the duodenum most, so iron deficiency is a common, and sometimes the only, sign of the disease.
whyNot: Correct.
Cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum take up vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor, not iron.
Gastric acid helps keep iron soluble, but celiac disease does not affect the stomach.
The colon absorbs water, salts, and short-chain fatty acids, but very little iron.

dx: Acute myeloid leukemia evolving from myelodysplasia in an adolescent with Fanconi anemia
case: A 15-year-old boy with Fanconi anemia is brought to the physician because of fatigue, fever, and bleeding gums for 2 weeks. He is short for his age, has an absent left thumb, and has several café-au-lait spots. A marrow biopsy 1 year ago showed myelodysplasia with 8% blasts and monosomy 7. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F). Hemoglobin concentration is 7.2 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), leukocyte count is 18,500/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) with 42% blasts, and platelet count is 14,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). A bone marrow aspirate shows 38% myeloblasts, some with Auer rods. Blasts are positive for myeloperoxidase. The diagnosis is acute myeloid leukemia arising from myelodysplasia in Fanconi anemia.

questions.stem: He is prepared for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. His conditioning dose of cyclophosphamide is a small fraction of the dose used for other patients. Which of the following best explains this adjustment?
options: Faster hepatic activation of the drug to toxic metabolites
Failure to repair the DNA interstrand crosslinks it forms
Absent telomerase activity in his hematopoietic stem cells
Inability to excise thymine dimers from damaged DNA
approach: Fanconi anemia genes encode proteins that repair DNA interstrand crosslinks.
Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide work by forming these crosslinks.
His cells cannot repair the damage, so standard doses would cause severe toxicity to all tissues.
questions.why: Fanconi anemia is usually autosomal recessive and results from mutations in the FANC pathway, which removes interstrand DNA crosslinks. Without it, crosslinks stall replication, leading to chromosome breaks, stem cell loss, marrow failure, and malignant clones such as myelodysplasia and AML. The same defect makes patients highly sensitive to crosslinking agents, which is why the diagnostic test measures chromosome breaks after diepoxybutane or mitomycin C exposure. Conditioning regimens are therefore reduced sharply.
whyNot: Fanconi anemia does not speed hepatic drug activation. The problem is repair of the DNA damage the drug causes.
Correct.
Defective telomere maintenance causes dyskeratosis congenita, another inherited marrow failure syndrome.
Failure to excise thymine dimers is a nucleotide excision repair defect, as in xeroderma pigmentosum, and causes sensitivity to ultraviolet light.

topics: Fanconi anemia and DNA crosslink repair

questions.stem: His marrow biopsy 1 year ago showed 8% blasts. Which of the following findings in that sample would best indicate dysplastic granulocyte development?
options: Toxic granulation with Döhle bodies
Increased eosinophil and basophil precursors
Bilobed, hypogranular neutrophils
Increased myelocytes with orderly maturation
approach: Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal disorders with ineffective blood cell production and abnormal-looking cells.
In the granulocyte line, dysplasia shows as neutrophils with too few lobes and too few granules.
Blasts below 20% fit myelodysplasia, and 20% or more defines AML.
questions.why: In myelodysplastic syndromes, a clone of marrow cells matures abnormally, so cells die in the marrow and the blood shows cytopenias. Typical dysplastic neutrophils have two lobes or a single nucleus and few granules (pseudo-Pelger-Huët cells). Erythroid dysplasia may include ringed sideroblasts. The disease is seen mostly in older adults or after alkylating agents or radiation, and in inherited marrow failure such as Fanconi anemia, and it can progress to AML.
whyNot: Toxic granulation and Döhle bodies are reactive changes in neutrophils during severe infection.
Increased eosinophil and basophil precursors suggest chronic myeloid leukemia.
Correct.
Increased myelocytes with orderly maturation suggest a reactive left shift or chronic myeloid leukemia, not dysplasia.

questions.stem: Which of the following patterns of granulocytes on his current blood smear best supports acute myeloid leukemia rather than a left shift from severe infection?
options: More bands and metamyelocytes, with toxic granulation
All stages from myeloblast to neutrophil, peaking at myelocytes
Hypersegmented neutrophils with oval macrocytes
Many blasts and mature neutrophils, few stages between
approach: Recall the order: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, segmented neutrophil.
A left shift adds the stages just before mature cells, mostly bands and metamyelocytes.
AML shows a gap: many blasts plus leftover mature neutrophils, with few cells in between.
questions.why: Normal granulocytes mature from myeloblast through promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, and band to segmented neutrophil. In infection, the marrow releases cells earlier, so bands and metamyelocytes rise in an orderly left shift. In AML, the leukemic blasts fail to mature, so the blood shows many blasts and a few residual mature neutrophils, with few intermediate forms (leukemic hiatus). Chronic myeloid leukemia shows all stages, with peaks of myelocytes and segmented neutrophils.
whyNot: More bands and metamyelocytes with toxic granulation is the reactive left shift of severe infection.
All stages with a myelocyte peak suggests chronic myeloid leukemia.
Hypersegmented neutrophils with oval macrocytes suggest megaloblastic anemia.
Correct.

questions.stem: After induction chemotherapy abruptly halts his marrow output, his absolute neutrophil count falls within days, his platelet count reaches its low point after about a week, and his hemoglobin concentration falls only slowly. Which of the following sets of approximate circulating life spans best explains this sequence?
options: Neutrophils 6 hours; platelets 8 days; red cells 120 days
Neutrophils 6 hours; platelets 30 days; red cells 60 days
Neutrophils 3 days; platelets 8 days; red cells 30 days
Neutrophils 10 days; platelets 3 days; red cells 120 days
approach: When production stops, each cell line falls at a rate set by how long its cells survive in the blood.
Neutrophils circulate for only hours, platelets for about 7 to 10 days, and red cells for about 120 days.
So neutropenia comes first, then thrombocytopenia, and anemia develops last.
questions.why: Neutrophils leave the blood for tissues within hours, with a circulating half-life of about 6 to 8 hours, so their count drops within days once the marrow reserve is used. Platelets survive about 7 to 10 days, so their count bottoms out in about a week. Red cells live about 120 days, so only about 1% are lost each day and hemoglobin falls slowly. This is why fever from neutropenia and bleeding from thrombocytopenia appear before anemia after marrow suppression.
whyNot: Correct.
Platelets live about 8 days rather than 30, and red cells live about 120 days rather than 60.
Neutrophils circulate for hours, not days, and red cells live much longer than 30 days.
Neutrophils do not outlive platelets in the blood. This order would make thrombocytopenia appear first.
